passages.title: The Particle That Passes Through Earth
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Every second, enormous numbers of neutrinos pass through your body and continue through Earth. They arrive from the Sun, from exploding stars, and from reactions high in the atmosphere. Yet you do not feel them. A neutrino has no electric charge and interacts with ordinary matter through forces that act only at extremely short range. Most neutrinos cross atoms without disturbing them.

That indifference makes neutrinos valuable messengers and difficult objects to study. Light from the center of the Sun may take a very long time to work outward, repeatedly meeting charged particles. Neutrinos leave almost immediately, carrying information about reactions in the solar core. However, the same weak interaction that lets them escape also lets them pass unnoticed through a laboratory.

Researchers answer this problem with scale and patience. Some detectors use huge tanks of water or other clear materials, placed deep underground to screen out more common particles. On rare occasions, a neutrino strikes a particle in the tank. The collision produces a faint pattern of light that sensitive instruments record. Scientists then compare many such flashes, their directions, and their energies. No single flash tells the whole story. Evidence emerges from a large collection of unlikely events. A neutrino detector therefore works by accepting an apparent contradiction: to observe particles that barely touch matter, researchers give them an immense amount of matter to cross.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Neutrinos rarely interact with matter, so scientists use enormous protected detectors to capture enough rare collisions to study them.
Neutrinos are visible forms of light that travel slowly from the center of the Sun.
Underground tanks prevent neutrinos from entering laboratories and damaging instruments.
A single neutrino flash reveals exactly where and when a distant star exploded.
questions.explanation: The passage links the neutrino’s weak interaction to both its value as a messenger and the need for very large detectors.

questions.stem: Why are neutrinos able to carry relatively direct information from the solar core?
choices: They store sunlight inside their electric charge until reaching Earth.
They can leave the core without repeatedly colliding with charged matter.
They move outward only after ordinary light has cleared a path.
They are produced in underground tanks rather than inside the Sun.
questions.explanation: The text contrasts neutrinos with light, which may repeatedly meet charged particles before it escapes the Sun.

questions.stem: In the phrase “That indifference makes neutrinos valuable messengers,” what does “indifference” mean?
choices: their inability to travel beyond Earth
their changing direction whenever they meet light
their tendency to pass through matter with almost no interaction
their usefulness only when no detector is present
questions.explanation: Here “indifference” describes neutrinos behaving as though most surrounding matter were not there.

questions.stem: What is one purpose of placing some neutrino detectors deep underground?
choices: to move the detector closer to the center of the Sun
to make neutrinos gain an electric charge before entering the tank
to prevent the clear material in the tank from producing any light
to screen out more common particles that could confuse the measurement
questions.explanation: The passage states that underground placement screens out more common particles, making rare neutrino signals easier to identify.

lesson.strategy: Follow the cause-and-effect chain: weak interaction allows escape, escape carries information, and weak interaction also makes detection rare. The final paragraph resolves that difficulty through scale, shielding, and many observations.

signals.means: This establishes the property that drives both the opportunity and the experimental problem.
This signal turns one feature into two opposite consequences: easy escape and hard detection.
These words introduce the practical answer to events that happen only rarely.

vocab.inContext: nearly chargeless particles that interact only weakly with ordinary matter
reduce unwanted signals so the rarer target events are easier to distinguish
two claims that seem opposed but are reconciled by the detector design

skillTips.main-idea: Build the main idea around the repeated property of weak interaction and both consequences the text draws from it.
skillTips.inference: For an inference, connect the comparison with light to the statement that neutrinos leave the solar core almost immediately.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read “indifference” as a metaphor, then replace it with the literal particle behavior described in the prior paragraph.
skillTips.detail: For detail questions, return to the detector paragraph and distinguish shielding from the tank’s collision-recording role.

passages.title: Gladys West Measures the Earth
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Gladys West grew up on a farm in Virginia. She excelled in mathematics at school. After college, she joined a United States Navy laboratory in 1956. Few women there did complex calculations.

West studied information sent by satellites. Earth is not a perfect ball, so finding its exact shape requires many measurements. West helped turn satellite observations into mathematical models of the planet. She checked results and improved the calculations as information arrived.

Those models later supported the Global Positioning System, or GPS. A phone can show a location only because satellites and receivers agree on a detailed model of Earth. West did not build a map app. Her patient work created part of the mathematical foundation beneath it. Years later, her contribution became widely known. Her story shows that a familiar tool may rest on careful work most users never see.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Gladys West designed the first phone that could display a map.
Gladys West’s careful satellite calculations helped build the Earth models that later supported GPS.
A Navy laboratory discovered that Earth is a perfect ball.
GPS became accurate only after satellites stopped sending measurements.
questions.explanation: The passage traces West’s mathematical work from satellite data to the Earth models used by GPS.

questions.stem: Why did West need many measurements to model Earth?
choices: The laboratory had no satellites.
Phones changed location too quickly.
Earth is not a perfect ball.
She wanted to draw every road by hand.
questions.explanation: The text directly explains that Earth’s uneven shape requires many measurements.

questions.stem: What does “foundation” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: the concrete floor of a laboratory
a prize given for public service
a drawing of the Virginia farm
an underlying part that later work depends on
questions.explanation: West’s models were an underlying basis for later GPS technology, not a building floor.

questions.stem: Where did West begin working in 1956?
choices: at a United States Navy laboratory
at a company that made phones
at a satellite launch site in space
at the farm where she grew up
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says she joined a United States Navy laboratory in 1956.

lesson.strategy: Read this biography as a chain from early skill to hidden impact. Notice the contrast between the familiar GPS result and the careful mathematical work underneath it.

signals.means: This begins the path from West’s early strength in mathematics to her later career.
This explains why a simple model would not be accurate enough.

signals.phrase: did not build a map app
signals.means: This contrast separates West’s foundational work from the tool users see.

vocab.inContext: careful uses of numbers to solve or measure something
mathematical descriptions used to represent Earth’s shape
an underlying part on which later technology depends

skillTips.main-idea: Choose a main idea that connects West’s calculations to GPS rather than focusing only on her childhood or workplace.
skillTips.inference: Use the sentence about Earth’s shape to explain why one simple measurement would not be enough.
skillTips.vocabulary: For “foundation,” use the nearby phrase “beneath it” and the later tool that depends on her work.
skillTips.detail: Keep the timeline straight: farm and school come first, the Navy laboratory follows, and broad recognition comes later.

passages.title: The Coupon Only Some People Use
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A grocery store could lower the price of soup for everyone. Instead, it prints a coupon. Any shopper may use it, but only some do. They must notice the offer, save it, and remember to present it. Those small tasks take time.

The coupon lets the store charge two prices for the same can. Shoppers who care strongly about saving money may accept the extra effort and pay less. Shoppers who value convenience more may pay the regular price. The product is unchanged; what differs is each buyer’s willingness to exchange time for a discount.

This method can help a store attract price-sensitive customers without cutting every sale. It does not prove that one group is wiser. A busy shopper may reasonably skip the coupon, while another shopper may enjoy searching for deals. Digital coupons can reduce the effort, although an account or app may create a different barrier. The important point is that the discount is not separated by chance alone. It asks customers to reveal something through what they are willing to do.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Coupons change the soup inside a can for shoppers who enjoy discounts.
Every shopper who ignores a coupon is making an unreasonable choice.
Coupons let a store offer a lower price mainly to shoppers willing to spend effort to claim it.
Digital coupons remove every barrier between a customer and a discount.
questions.explanation: The entire passage explains how the task of claiming a coupon separates shoppers by their willingness to trade effort for savings.

questions.stem: Why might a busy shopper skip a coupon?
choices: The coupon makes the soup taste different from the regular product.
Stores forbid busy people from using printed discounts.
A coupon always costs more than the amount it saves.
The saved money may be worth less to that shopper than the required time and attention.
questions.explanation: The passage says convenience can matter more than the discount, so skipping it may be a reasonable tradeoff.

questions.stem: In this passage, what does “price-sensitive” mean?
choices: likely to change a buying choice in response to price
unable to read a printed price correctly
interested only in products sold online
required to pay the regular price
questions.explanation: Price-sensitive customers care strongly about savings and may do extra work to obtain a lower price.

questions.stem: What new barrier can a digital coupon create?
choices: It changes the product into a digital file.
It may require an account or an app.
It forces every price to be lower.
It prevents a store from tracking sales.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph names an account or app as a different kind of barrier.

lesson.strategy: Track what remains the same (the soup) and what changes: the effort needed to reach the lower price. The final paragraph adds an important qualification: different choices can both be reasonable.

signals.means: This names the nonmoney cost attached to receiving the lower price.
This directs attention away from quality and toward differences between buyers.
This phrase warns against turning an economic sorting method into a moral judgment.

vocab.inContext: ease and saved effort that may matter more than a small discount
likely to respond strongly when a price changes
a requirement that makes access harder for some shoppers

skillTips.main-idea: State the main idea as a mechanism: coupons sort buyers by the effort they will exchange for a lower price.
skillTips.inference: Infer a shopper’s choice by comparing the value of saved money with the value of time, not by calling either shopper careless.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the behavior of customers who search for savings to unlock the meaning of “price-sensitive.”
skillTips.detail: When locating details, separate the printed coupon tasks from the account or app required by some digital coupons.

passages.title: Why Shared Meals Matter
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A shared meal does not need matching plates or a recipe. Its value begins with a fact: several people place their attention in the same room at the same time. They pass food, notice who needs water, and adjust the pace so nobody is left behind.

That coordination creates small chances to know one another. A story can continue after the bowl is passed. A quiet person may enter the conversation because there is no need to announce a formal topic. Even disagreement can become less sharp when everyone is also solving the practical problem of dividing bread or clearing space.

Still, it would be careless to treat one kind of table as a universal picture of family. Some people eat alone because of work, distance, disability, grief, or preference. Others share food with friends, coworkers, neighbors, or a changing household. Time and money can make daily gatherings impossible. The useful principle is broader than dinner. Relationships need repeated moments in which attention is not accidental. A meal is one durable way to create them, but a walk, a call, or tea during a night shift can perform similar work. The form may change; making room for one another remains.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the essay?
choices: A proper family must eat a formal dinner together every evening.
People solve disagreements only when they divide bread equally.
Eating alone always shows that a person lacks close relationships.
Shared meals matter because they create repeated, coordinated attention, but other inclusive routines can serve the same purpose.
questions.explanation: The essay values the attention created by meals while explicitly widening the principle to other relationships and routines.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention a walk, a call, and tea during a night shift?
choices: to show that connection can be created through routines other than a meal
to argue that food makes conversation impossible
to list activities that require matching plates
to prove that coworkers are always closer than families
questions.explanation: These examples carry the essay’s broader principle beyond a traditional dinner table.

questions.stem: What does “durable” mean in the phrase “one durable way”?
choices: expensive to organize correctly
able to remain useful over time
formal enough for a celebration
unlikely to include conversation
questions.explanation: The meal is described as a repeated practice that can keep creating moments of attention over time.

questions.stem: What practical activity does the essay say may soften disagreement?
choices: choosing a formal topic before speaking
making every person eat at the same speed
dividing bread or clearing space together
keeping quiet until the meal is finished
questions.explanation: The second paragraph specifically pairs disagreement with the shared tasks of dividing bread and clearing space.

lesson.strategy: The essay moves from a concrete table to a broader claim about attention. Read the third paragraph as a qualification: it protects the central value while rejecting one narrow image of how connection must look.

signals.means: This phrase turns simple meal tasks into the essay’s claim about relationship building.
This marks the qualification that prevents the claim from becoming a rule for every household.
This sentence names the move from shared food to repeated attention in many forms.

vocab.inContext: people adjusting their actions so a shared activity works
true or suitable for every person and household
able to continue being useful over time

skillTips.main-idea: A complete main idea must carry both halves: shared attention matters, and a meal is one form rather than the only form.
skillTips.inference: Treat the final examples as evidence for a broader category, then name the common work they all perform.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use “repeated moments” and “remains” to see that “durable” describes something that lasts.
skillTips.detail: For a detail, return to the middle paragraph and identify the ordinary task linked directly to softer disagreement.

passages.title: The Banyan and the Bamboo
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A banyan spread its branches over half the village square. Its roots descended from the limbs and thickened into pillars. Beside it grew a stand of bamboo, narrow and restless in every breeze.

“Strength means holding your place,” the banyan told the bamboo. “One hard wind, and you will bow to the ground.”

The bamboo answered, “Strength means returning after you bend.” Neither persuaded the other. Then a slow season without rain settled over the village. The banyan reached deep water through its many roots and kept a pool of shade beneath its crown. The bamboo’s shallow ground dried. Its leaves curled, and several stems failed.

Months later, rain returned with a violent storm. Water loosened the soil, and wind pulled at the banyan’s wide crown. One great limb broke, though the rooted pillars kept the tree standing. The bamboo bent nearly flat. When the storm passed, most stems rose again, but they rose into a square still shaded by the banyan. Each had survived a danger suited to its own design. The banyan stopped calling bending weakness. The bamboo stopped calling depth stubbornness. After that, when young trees asked which kind of strength was best, both answered, “Ask first what is coming.”

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the fable?
choices: Different forms of strength meet different dangers, so judging one design without considering the challenge is foolish.
Deep roots make every plant stronger than flexible stems in every kind of weather.
The banyan and bamboo survive only because the village protects them from storms.
Young trees should copy whichever plant appears largest in the village square.
questions.explanation: The drought favors depth, the storm favors flexibility, and both plants revise their one-sided judgment at the end.

questions.stem: Why does neither plant fully win the argument?
choices: Both plants leave the square before the weather changes.
Each plant is tested by a different danger that reveals both strength and weakness.
The bamboo develops roots identical to the banyan’s roots.
The banyan becomes narrow enough to bend flat in the storm.
questions.explanation: The paired trials divide the evidence: the banyan handles drought better, while the bamboo handles strong wind better.

questions.stem: In the final advice, what does “what is coming” refer to?
choices: the next plant that will enter the square
the age of the tree asking the question
the particular kind of challenge that must be faced
the direction from which villagers will arrive
questions.explanation: The plants have learned that the best form of strength depends on whether the threat is drought, wind, or something else.

questions.stem: What keeps the banyan standing after its great limb breaks?
choices: the bamboo stems
the village wall
its curled leaves
its rooted pillars
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says that the rooted pillars keep the banyan standing despite the broken limb.

lesson.strategy: Treat the drought and storm as a matched test. Each event changes which plant looks stronger, so the moral cannot praise one trait alone; it must explain why context changes the judgment.

signals.means: The banyan defines strength too narrowly before either plant has faced both tests.

signals.phrase: Strength means returning after you bend
signals.means: The bamboo offers an opposing definition that is also incomplete by itself.
The final answer replaces a contest between traits with attention to the actual challenge.

vocab.inContext: grew downward from the banyan’s branches toward the ground
convinced the other plant to accept an argument
well matched to a particular danger or purpose

skillTips.main-idea: Frame the main idea around two tests and two useful traits, not around a victory by either plant.
skillTips.inference: Infer why the debate remains unsettled by comparing the outcome of the dry season with the outcome of the storm.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read “what is coming” beside the two weather events; it means the challenge, not another character.
skillTips.detail: For the storm detail, distinguish the limb that breaks from the rooted pillars that keep the whole tree upright.

passages.title: Does Work Need a Larger Meaning?
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
People often ask whether their work is meaningful, but the question can hide different demands. One person wants work to improve other lives. Another wants to master a craft. A third values the freedom that wages provide outside work. If these aims are treated as one thing, a job may be judged empty because it does not satisfy every aim.

Social contribution matters. Work joins a person to needs beyond private preference: repairing water pipes, teaching a language, preparing a room for strangers. Yet contribution is not enough. A useful job organized without respect can damage the worker. Nor does a grand mission excuse exhaustion or unfair treatment.

Meaning may also grow from chosen commitment. A translator can care about exact sentences; a baker can care about a reliable loaf. The object need not transform history. Through sustained attention, work becomes a place where judgment and skill take form. But this idea has a danger. Calling every hardship a source of growth can turn endurance into an obligation and conceal conditions that should change.

Perhaps work does not need one larger meaning. It needs honest language about the goods it actually provides and the costs it imposes. For some, work will be a vocation. For others, it will support meaning located in family, art, faith, friendship, or rest. Neither pattern is automatically shallow. The philosophical task is not to force one answer onto every life, but to ask which values a particular job serves, which it frustrates, and whether that balance can be defended.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Only work that directly transforms society can give a person a meaningful life.
Work can carry several kinds of value, but no single source of meaning should be forced onto every job or every life.
Mastering a craft always justifies unfair treatment and needless exhaustion.
A job has no value unless a worker experiences it as a lifelong vocation.
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes contribution, mastery, wages, and life outside work, then argues for an honest case-by-case balance.

questions.stem: Why does the author warn against calling every hardship a source of growth?
choices: It proves that skill never develops through difficult practice.
It makes socially useful jobs disappear from the economy.
That language can hide harmful conditions that ought to be changed.
It requires every worker to choose a grand historical mission.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says that praising endurance can conceal conditions that deserve change.

questions.stem: What does “vocation” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: a short break taken between two work shifts
the wages that make leisure possible
a rule requiring every job to serve strangers
work experienced as a deep calling or central purpose
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts work as a vocation with work that supports meaning found elsewhere, so vocation means a calling.

questions.stem: Which example illustrates meaning through careful mastery rather than a grand mission?
choices: a baker caring about a reliable loaf
a person using wages outside the workplace
a worker enduring unfair treatment
a job being judged by every aim at once
questions.explanation: The baker’s reliable loaf appears in the paragraph about chosen commitment, judgment, and skill.

lesson.strategy: Separate the passage’s candidates for meaning: contribution, mastery, material support, and values outside work. Then track each qualification, because the conclusion depends on refusing to let any single good excuse every cost.

signals.means: This warns that one familiar question contains several distinct standards.
This qualification prevents social usefulness from excusing disrespect or harm.

signals.phrase: Perhaps work does not need one larger meaning
signals.means: The conclusion replaces a universal answer with an honest evaluation of particular values and costs.

vocab.inContext: work that serves needs or benefits beyond the worker’s private preference
a deliberately sustained investment of attention and care
work understood as a calling or central purpose in a life

skillTips.main-idea: A strong main idea includes several legitimate kinds of value and the rejection of one mandatory meaning for all work.
skillTips.inference: For inference, ask what bad condition becomes harder to see when endurance itself is always praised as growth.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the contrast with meaning in family, art, faith, friendship, or rest to define “vocation” as a calling.
skillTips.detail: Match examples to arguments: pipes and teaching show contribution, while the translator and baker show mastery.

passages.title: Putting a Name on a Feeling
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A feeling can arrive before its name. Your shoulders tighten, thoughts race, or you want to leave. Saying only “I feel bad” gives little guidance. A precise label can separate worry from anger, embarrassment, disappointment, or tiredness.

Naming a feeling does not make it vanish. It can make the experience easier to examine. If the feeling is disappointment, the mind can ask what hope was not met. If it is embarrassment, the concern may be how other people saw an event. Different names point toward different causes.

Labels can also be wrong. A hungry person may call simple irritation anger at a friend. That is why a useful label remains a working guess, not a final verdict. The goal is not to force every feeling into a neat box. It is to replace one blurred signal with a clearer question: what, exactly, is happening here?

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Every uncomfortable feeling has one permanent name that cannot be mistaken.
Calling a feeling bad is the fastest way to remove it completely.
Giving a feeling a careful, tentative name can clarify its possible cause without making the feeling disappear.
Physical signs always reveal exactly which emotion a person has.
questions.explanation: The passage presents labels as useful clues while warning that they remain revisable guesses.

questions.stem: Why might the word “disappointment” be more useful than “bad”?
choices: It guarantees that other people caused the feeling.
It proves that the person is actually hungry.
It prevents the feeling from returning later.
It points toward a hope that may not have been met.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph links disappointment with asking which hope was not met.

questions.stem: What does “verdict” mean in the phrase “not a final verdict”?
choices: a fixed conclusion or judgment
a physical sign in the shoulders
a question asked by a friend
a feeling that vanishes quickly
questions.explanation: The label is described as a working guess rather than a fixed final conclusion.

questions.stem: What can hunger sometimes be mistaken for?
choices: embarrassment about an event
anger at a friend
a hope that was not met
a wish to leave a room
questions.explanation: The final paragraph gives the example of a hungry person calling irritation anger at a friend.

lesson.strategy: Follow the movement from a vague signal to a more precise question. The last paragraph supplies the limit: emotion words are tools for inquiry, not permanent judgments.

signals.means: This shows why the broad label “bad” is not useful enough.
This corrects the idea that naming an emotion is a quick cure.
This describes the label as useful but open to correction.

vocab.inContext: a specific word used to identify the kind of feeling
look at an experience carefully to understand it
a final conclusion or judgment

skillTips.main-idea: The main idea needs both the benefit of precise naming and the warning that a label may change.
skillTips.inference: Link each emotion word to the cause the passage places beside it rather than importing a cause from outside.
skillTips.vocabulary: The contrast between “working guess” and “final” reveals that “verdict” means a fixed conclusion.
skillTips.detail: For details, distinguish the hunger example in the last paragraph from the disappointment and embarrassment examples above.

passages.title: The Printer That Builds in Layers
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A three-dimensional printer begins with a digital model. Software divides the model into thin horizontal slices. Each slice becomes an instruction for one level of the physical object.

In a common kind of printer, a nozzle heats a plastic thread until it softens. The nozzle moves across a platform, placing a narrow line where the first slice says material should go. The plastic cools and becomes firm. Then the machine raises its working position slightly and lays down the next slice. Layer follows layer until the full shape appears.

This method can create curves, hollow spaces, and custom parts without cutting them from a solid block. It also has limits. A fresh layer may sag if nothing supports it from below, so some designs need temporary support material. The surface can show fine ridges where the layers meet. Printing can also be slow because every line must be placed in order. The machine does not simply pull a finished object from a file. It translates a digital shape into a careful sequence of small deposits.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A three-dimensional printer carves every object from one solid block of plastic.
Digital models remove the need for ordered instructions during printing.
Every printed object has a perfectly smooth surface and needs no support.
A three-dimensional printer turns a sliced digital model into an object by placing and cooling material one layer at a time.
questions.explanation: The passage follows the full translation from digital slices to repeated physical deposits and also notes the method’s limits.

questions.stem: Why might a design need temporary support material?
choices: A new layer can sag when there is nothing beneath it.
The digital model has too many colors to print.
The nozzle must remain cold while it moves.
The platform cuts each layer from a block.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph directly links unsupported fresh layers with sagging.

questions.stem: What does “deposits” mean in the final sentence?
choices: payments made to buy the printer
small amounts of material placed in position
files removed from a computer
empty spaces inside an object
questions.explanation: The printer builds by placing narrow lines of softened material, so deposits are the amounts it puts down.

questions.stem: What happens immediately after the plastic is placed for a slice?
choices: The model is divided into slices.
The finished object is cut apart.
It cools and becomes firm.
The nozzle removes the platform.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the placed plastic cools and becomes firm before the next layer is added.

lesson.strategy: Read the second paragraph as a repeated cycle: heat, place, cool, rise, repeat. The last paragraph contrasts useful geometric freedom with limits caused by the same layer-by-layer method.

signals.means: This is the digital preparation that turns a whole shape into ordered instructions.
This compresses the repeated building cycle into one clear sequence signal.
This marks the turn from what layered printing enables to the problems it can create.

vocab.inContext: the moving tip that heats and places a narrow line of plastic
bend or droop because there is not enough support below
small amounts of material placed in chosen positions

skillTips.main-idea: Include both the sliced digital plan and the repeated placement of physical material in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the need for support by picturing what happens when softened material is laid over empty space.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the verb “placing” earlier in the passage to identify deposits as material put down by the nozzle.
skillTips.detail: To answer a sequence detail, trace one slice only and keep digital preparation separate from cooling on the platform.

passages.title: The Shoes Outside Door Twelve
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Every Thursday evening, shoes gathered outside Door Twelve. Some were polished, some muddy, and one pair was bright yellow. Mara lived across the hall. She heard many voices behind the door, rising and falling in a rhythm she could not understand.

She began imagining explanations. Perhaps the apartment held secret auctions. Perhaps the tenants repaired radios and tested them at once. When a cardboard sign appeared beside the shoes, Mara saw only unfamiliar writing and became more uneasy.

One rainy Thursday, the owner of the yellow shoes knocked on Mara’s door. He held a wet bag whose bottom had torn. Workbooks covered the floor. Each showed the same two sentences in different alphabets. “Could you help me gather these?” he asked. “Our free language class starts soon.”

Mara carried the books inside. The shoes belonged to nurses, cooks, grandparents, and two teenagers. They practiced greetings, taking turns so everyone could finish. The sign welcomed learners in six languages. Mara had mistaken a room designed to make strangers understandable for something mysterious. The next week, her shoes stood outside Door Twelve. She offered to help with conversation practice and began learning the yellow-shoed man’s first language too.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: Mara’s suspicion about a neighbor’s gathering changes into participation when she learns it is an inclusive language class.
Mara discovers that Door Twelve contains a secret auction for unusual shoes.
A language teacher asks Mara to repair a bag before anyone may enter class.
The residents stop meeting because Mara cannot read the sign outside the door.
questions.explanation: The story’s arc moves from uneasy guessing to evidence, understanding, and mutual participation.

questions.stem: Why does Mara join the class the following week?
choices: She wants to discover which student owns the muddy shoes.
Seeing its welcoming purpose replaces her suspicion and gives her a way to contribute and learn.
The owner orders her to translate all six versions of the sign.
She hopes the group will begin repairing radios instead.
questions.explanation: After entering, Mara sees people patiently helping one another communicate, so her final choice follows from new understanding.

questions.stem: What does “gather” mean when the man asks Mara for help?
choices: bring every class member into the hall
understand an unfamiliar alphabet
pick up and collect the scattered workbooks
hold a secret meeting in an apartment
questions.explanation: The wet bag has torn and workbooks cover the floor, so gathering means collecting them.

questions.stem: What do the workbooks show?
choices: prices for objects sold at an auction
instructions for repairing old radios
a list of tenants who may enter Door Twelve
the same two sentences in different alphabets
questions.explanation: The third paragraph describes the workbooks as carrying two matching sentences in different alphabets.

lesson.strategy: Track the evidence Mara has, then separate it from the explanations she invents. The fallen workbooks form the turn: after that concrete clue, the same voices, sign, and shoes receive a new meaning.

signals.means: This signals that the secret auction and radio repair are guesses rather than evidence.
This direct statement overturns Mara’s imagined explanations.
This time shift reveals that understanding has changed Mara’s behavior, not only her opinion.

vocab.inContext: the repeated pattern in how the voices rise and fall together
worried because the unfamiliar gathering seems suspicious
pick up and collect items scattered across the floor

skillTips.main-idea: The main idea should name Mara’s mistaken suspicion, the revelation, and her changed behavior at the end.
skillTips.inference: Infer Mara’s reason for joining from what she observes inside: patience, welcome, and mutual understanding.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the torn bag and books on the floor to choose the physical meaning of “gather.”
skillTips.detail: For details, keep the evidence in the workbooks separate from Mara’s earlier invented stories about auctions and radios.

passages.title: The Mapmaker of the Ottoman Sea
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In 1513, the Ottoman sailor and mapmaker Piri Reis completed a map of the Atlantic world. Only part of it survives. The fragment shows western coasts of Europe and Africa, islands in the Atlantic, and parts of the Americas. Its painted ships, rulers, animals, and notes make it both a navigational document and a record of what one learned sailor believed about distant places.

Piri Reis did not claim to have measured every coast himself. Notes on the map describe his use of older and newer sources, including Portuguese charts, an Arabic map, ancient geography, and a chart connected in his account with Christopher Columbus. Combining them was skilled work, but it also carried their disagreements and errors forward. A copied coastline could become more convincing without becoming more accurate.

The surviving fragment is sometimes treated as a mysterious object containing impossible knowledge. Its real importance is more instructive. It shows how geographic information moved among sailors and empires around the Mediterranean and Atlantic. Maps were assembled arguments: a mapmaker selected reports, fitted different scales together, and decided which uncertainty to leave visible. Piri Reis later produced a detailed sailing guide to Mediterranean ports, showing his practical knowledge of the sea. His 1513 map matters not because it escaped its time, but because it captures that time’s remarkable network of observation, copying, travel, and judgment.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Piri Reis personally measured every coastline shown on his complete surviving world map.
Piri Reis’s surviving map shows how a skilled mapmaker combined circulating sources, including their uncertainty, into a view of the early Atlantic world.
The 1513 map proves that Ottoman sailors possessed geographic knowledge from the modern era.
Painted ships and animals made the map decorative but useless for understanding history.
questions.explanation: The passage emphasizes selection and combination of sources, the limits inherited from them, and the map’s value as evidence of its own time.

questions.stem: Why does the author call maps “assembled arguments”?
choices: Every map was presented orally in a court before sailors could use it.
Painted rulers argued with one another in the map’s illustrations.
Mapmakers chose among reports and decided how uncertain pieces would fit together.
A chart became accurate automatically when it included many sources.
questions.explanation: The sentence after the phrase explains the choices involved in selecting, scaling, and displaying uncertain information.

questions.stem: What does “fragment” mean in this passage?
choices: a deliberate error added to a coastline
a guide listing Mediterranean ports
a scale shared by all early charts
a surviving part of a larger object
questions.explanation: The passage says only part of the 1513 map survives and then calls that surviving part a fragment.

questions.stem: Which kind of source does the passage say Piri Reis used?
choices: Portuguese charts
satellite photographs
railway surveys
modern ocean-depth scans
questions.explanation: Portuguese charts appear in the list of sources described by notes on the map.

lesson.strategy: Read the map as a historical process, not a puzzle detached from its century. Follow the verbs describing source work (used, combining, selected, fitted) and keep skill separate from perfect accuracy.

signals.means: This establishes that readers are studying one fragment rather than a complete world map.
This corrects the assumption that Piri Reis personally surveyed every coast.
This marks the turn from sensational mystery to the map’s historical value.

vocab.inContext: a surviving part of the larger map
made or used to help guide travel by sea
built by selecting and fitting material from several sources

skillTips.main-idea: The main idea must include both skilled synthesis and inherited uncertainty; either half alone is incomplete.
skillTips.inference: Infer the meaning of “assembled arguments” from the specific mapmaking choices listed immediately afterward.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the opening contrast between the completed map and the part that survives to define “fragment.”
skillTips.detail: For source details, return to the second paragraph and reject technologies that did not exist in 1513.

passages.title: The Sea Star That Reshaped a Shore
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
On a rocky Pacific shore, mussels can crowd together so tightly that little bare stone remains. They are excellent competitors for space. Yet a familiar predator can keep that strength from turning into total control: a sea star that pulls open mussel shells and feeds on the animals inside.

Ecologist Robert Paine tested this relationship on a section of coast. He repeatedly removed the predatory sea stars from one area while leaving another area alone for comparison. Without the predator, mussels spread. Several other species lost places to attach, feed, or shelter, and the community became less diverse. The sea star was not the most numerous animal on the rocks. Its influence came from which animal it ate.

This experiment helped shape the idea of a keystone species. In an arch, a keystone is one stone, but its position helps support the whole structure. In an ecosystem, a keystone species has an effect much larger than its abundance might suggest. Removing it can reorganize relationships among many other species.

The label does not mean every predator is a keystone in every location. Food webs change across habitats and seasons, and later studies may reveal additional causes. Paine's result mattered because it joined a clear intervention to a broad ecological change. Instead of merely noticing that sea stars and diversity occurred together, he changed one factor and watched the shore respond.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Sea stars are always the most numerous animals in every coastal habitat.
Mussels disappear whenever a predator is removed from a rocky shore.
Removing a predatory sea star let mussels dominate, showing how one keystone species can strongly shape an entire shore community.
A keystone species is simply the largest species found in an ecosystem.
questions.explanation: The experiment connects removal, mussel expansion, and declining diversity to explain influence beyond abundance.

questions.stem: Why was the comparison area important?
choices: It gave the removed sea stars a new place to eat.
It prevented mussels from attaching to any rocks.
It proved seasons never affect coastal food webs.
It helped show what changed when sea stars were removed rather than when the shore was left alone.
questions.explanation: A comparison makes the intervention easier to distinguish from ordinary changes on the shore.

questions.stem: What does “intervention” mean here?
choices: a deliberate change made to test what happens
a list of all species living near the water
a stone placed at the top of an arch
a natural season in which mussels grow
questions.explanation: Paine deliberately removed one predator and observed the response, so the intervention was the tested change.

questions.stem: What happened after sea stars were removed?
choices: The rocks became permanently bare.
Mussels spread and several other species lost space.
Every predator became more abundant.
The comparison area was also cleared.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes mussel expansion followed by fewer places for other species.

lesson.strategy: Trace the experiment as cause and effect: removal changes predation, mussels gain space, and diversity falls. Then use the arch comparison to understand why abundance and influence are not the same measure.

signals.means: This phrase introduces the ecological consequences of the deliberate removal.
This contrast separates a species count from the size of its influence.
This marks the difference between observing a pattern and testing a cause.

vocab.inContext: organisms seeking the same limited resource, such as space on rock
a species whose ecological effect is unusually large for its abundance
a deliberate change introduced to test a possible cause

skillTips.main-idea: Build the main idea from the tested removal and its community-wide result, not from the arch image alone.
skillTips.inference: Infer the comparison area’s role by asking what evidence is needed to connect the removal with later change.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the nearby contrast with “merely noticing” to define intervention as an intentional test.
skillTips.detail: For the result, follow the order in paragraph two: sea stars leave, mussels spread, and other species lose space.

passages.title: Why an Orchestra Tunes First
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Before a concert, an orchestra makes a noisy wave of sound. Usually, one musician plays a steady note. Other players compare their own notes with it. They adjust their instruments until the pitches agree.

This step matters because instruments can drift out of tune. Heat, cold, and moisture may change strings or wood. A player may tighten a string or move a tuning slide. The goal is not to make every instrument sound alike. A flute and a cello should keep their own voices.

Instead, tuning gives the group a shared reference. When everyone agrees where one pitch belongs, chords fit together more clearly. The brief noise before the music is therefore not confusion. It is careful cooperation that helps many different sounds begin from the same point.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: An orchestra tunes to make every instrument sound exactly like a flute.
Musicians make random noise because they have forgotten the music.
Only string instruments can change when the room becomes warm.
An orchestra tunes so different instruments share a pitch reference before performing together.
questions.explanation: The passage explains how comparison with one note prepares varied instruments to play accurately together.

questions.stem: Why might an instrument drift out of tune?
choices: Heat, cold, or moisture can change its materials.
A chord always contains too many players.
The audience chooses a different melody.
The conductor removes every tuning slide.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph names temperature and moisture as causes.

questions.stem: What does “reference” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: a page listing the concert songs
a shared standard used for comparison
the special voice of a cello
a sound made only by strings
questions.explanation: Players compare their pitches with the steady note, which serves as a standard.

questions.stem: What may a player move to adjust some instruments?
choices: an audience chair
a sheet of tickets
a tuning slide
a concert curtain
questions.explanation: The passage names tightening a string and moving a tuning slide as adjustments.

lesson.strategy: Follow the sequence compare, adjust, agree. Then notice the contrast between preserving each instrument’s voice and sharing one pitch standard.

signals.means: This places tuning before the group begins the planned performance.
This corrects the mistaken idea that tuning erases differences among instruments.
This introduces the real purpose of the noisy preparation.

vocab.inContext: how high or low musical notes sound
change gradually away from the intended tuning
a standard that other notes can be compared with

skillTips.main-idea: Choose a main idea that connects the shared note with the group’s later performance.
skillTips.inference: Find causes of drifting in the second paragraph rather than guessing from concert behavior.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the earlier act of comparing notes to understand “reference” as a standard.
skillTips.detail: For an adjustment detail, locate the two actions a player may take after materials change.

passages.title: The Smell After Rain
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
After rain reaches dry ground, the air may carry an earthy smell called petrichor. The scent does not come from water alone. Plants leave oils on soil and stone during dry weather. Certain soil bacteria also produce a compound called geosmin.

When a raindrop hits a porous surface, tiny air bubbles can form beneath it. The bubbles rise through the drop and burst. They release a fine mist of particles into the air. Those particles can carry geosmin and plant oils toward a person's nose.

Light rain can produce the effect especially well because drops strike gently enough to trap bubbles. A hard downpour may wash material away before much becomes airborne. Wind, soil type, and the length of the dry spell also change what people smell. Petrichor is therefore not the odor of rain itself. It is a brief airborne mixture released when rain meets a particular landscape.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Petrichor forms when raindrops release soil compounds and plant oils into the air.
Rainwater creates a smell without touching soil, stone, plants, or bacteria.
Only hard downpours can carry geosmin toward a person’s nose.
Every landscape produces exactly the same scent after rain.
questions.explanation: The passage traces the scent from materials on the ground through bubbles and airborne particles.

questions.stem: Why can light rain produce a strong effect?
choices: It prevents soil bacteria from producing geosmin.
Its drops may trap bubbles without quickly washing the scented material away.
Its drops never touch porous ground.
It removes every plant oil before bubbles form.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph contrasts bubble-forming light rain with downpours that may wash material away.

questions.stem: What does “airborne” mean?
choices: stored deep under soil
created only by water
carried through the air
too heavy to move
questions.explanation: The particles travel into the air and toward a nose, so airborne means carried in air.

questions.stem: What compound is produced by certain soil bacteria?
choices: petrichor
oxygen
salt
geosmin
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph directly identifies geosmin as a compound made by some soil bacteria.

lesson.strategy: Trace the mechanism from ground materials to trapped bubbles, bursting droplets, and a nose. The final comparison explains why more rain does not always create more scent.

signals.phrase: does not come from water alone
signals.means: This redirects attention to oils and compounds already present on the ground.
This continues the physical sequence that carries scent-bearing particles upward.
This conclusion separates the smell of a reaction with a landscape from water itself.

vocab.inContext: the earthy scent noticed when rain reaches dry ground
a strongly scented compound produced by certain soil bacteria
lifted and carried through the surrounding air

skillTips.main-idea: Make the main idea explain how the scent travels, not merely when people notice it.
skillTips.inference: For the light-rain inference, combine bubble trapping with the contrast about material washing away.
skillTips.vocabulary: Follow the particles from the burst drop toward a nose to determine what “airborne” means.
skillTips.detail: Keep the terms distinct: bacteria produce geosmin, while petrichor names the overall earthy smell.

passages.title: Ellen Ochoa Carries Music to Orbit
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
As a child in California, Ellen Ochoa studied classical flute. She also became interested in mathematics and science, though she did not begin college expecting to be an astronaut. Curiosity led her toward physics and then electrical engineering.

Ochoa earned a doctorate and researched optical systems that could process information in images. She became an inventor on several patents. NASA selected her as an astronaut in 1990. Three years later, she became the first Hispanic woman to travel in space. Her shuttle crew studied Earth's atmosphere and the Sun's effects on it.

Ochoa brought a flute on her first mission. Playing in orbit joined an old discipline with a newer one. Music had trained her to listen closely, practice difficult passages, and improve through repetition. Engineering demanded another form of careful practice: testing ideas against evidence.

She eventually flew on four space missions and later became director of NASA's Johnson Space Center. Her path was not a straight childhood plan. It was a series of demanding interests that strengthened one another. The flute in orbit did not compete with science; it made visible the range of skills one explorer could carry.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the biography?
choices: Ellen Ochoa abandoned music before becoming interested in any kind of science.
Ellen Ochoa combined sustained interests in music and engineering on a path that led to invention, spaceflight, and leadership.
NASA selected Ochoa mainly because she could perform concerts in orbit.
Ochoa followed one unchanged plan to become an astronaut from early childhood.
questions.explanation: The biography links her developing interests and rejects the idea of a single straight path.

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the comparison between music and engineering?
choices: Neither field required Ochoa to test or revise her work.
Music supplied all the technical knowledge needed for spaceflight.
Both rewarded careful attention, practice, and improvement over time.
Engineering prevented her from continuing to play flute.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly pairs musical repetition with engineering tests against evidence.

questions.stem: What does “discipline” mean in the third paragraph?
choices: a punishment for making a mistake
a rule against music in space
a device used to process images
a field of skilled study and practice
questions.explanation: The sentence describes music and engineering as two practiced areas, so discipline means a field of study.

questions.stem: In what year did Ochoa first travel in space?
questions.explanation: NASA selected her in 1990, and the passage says she traveled in space three years later.

lesson.strategy: Read the biography as an accumulating path rather than a childhood destiny. Track how music, research, invention, flight, and leadership each contribute a different kind of preparation.

signals.means: This warns readers not to rewrite Ochoa’s path as a fixed plan from childhood.
This links astronaut selection in 1990 with her first spaceflight in 1993.
This states the author’s view that artistic and scientific abilities can reinforce one another.

vocab.inContext: involving light and the ways it can carry or process information
a field developed through focused study and practice
a repeated path around Earth or another object in space

skillTips.main-idea: Include both the range of Ochoa’s interests and the achievements that grew from them in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Base the inference on the parallel habits the passage assigns to musical and engineering practice.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the comparison of music with engineering to select the field-of-study meaning of “discipline.”
skillTips.detail: For the date, combine the stated selection year with the “three years later” transition.

passages.title: Money Sent Home
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A worker who moves to another city or country may regularly send part of each paycheck to relatives. Economists call such a transfer a remittance. For the household receiving it, the money can pay school fees, repair a roof, buy medicine, or soften the loss from a failed harvest.

A remittance is private money, but millions of transfers can shape a national economy. They bring funds into communities that may have few formal jobs or limited public support. Families often decide directly which need is most urgent. That flexibility is valuable, especially during a local emergency.

The same flow has costs and risks. The sender may accept lonely or dangerous work and have less money for housing in the new location. Fees charged by transfer services reduce what arrives. Exchange rates can also change the value received. A family that depends on one worker's income becomes vulnerable if that job disappears.

Remittances should not be mistaken for a complete development plan. A transfer can help a household immediately, while roads, schools, reliable banks, and safe employment require broader investment. Nor should recipients be described as passive. The transfer often belongs to a family strategy in which members divide work, caregiving, and risk across places. Money moves along that relationship, but so do obligations and choices.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Remittances are public taxes used only to build national roads and schools.
A worker who sends money always becomes financially secure in the new location.
Remittances can give families flexible support and affect economies, while also carrying fees, risks, and limits.
Families receiving transfers make no active choices about how the money is used.
questions.explanation: The passage balances household benefits with sender costs, transfer losses, dependency risks, and the need for public investment.

questions.stem: Why can remittances be especially useful during a local emergency?
choices: Exchange rates stop changing whenever an emergency begins.
Transfer companies remove all fees during difficult periods.
The money can be used only for one national project.
Families can direct the money toward the need they judge most urgent.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph connects direct family decisions and flexibility with emergency value.

questions.stem: What does “vulnerable” mean in the third paragraph?
choices: open to serious harm if circumstances change
guaranteed to receive more money
unable to choose how funds are spent
protected by several independent incomes
questions.explanation: Depending on one job creates exposure to loss if that job disappears.

questions.stem: What can reduce the amount of money that reaches a family?
choices: the family choosing an urgent need
fees charged by transfer services
a worker receiving a paycheck
caregiving shared across places
questions.explanation: The third paragraph directly says transfer fees reduce what arrives.

lesson.strategy: Separate the viewpoints of recipient, sender, and wider economy. Then follow the qualifications: a private transfer can be powerful without replacing safe work or public systems.

signals.means: This shifts the scale from one household to an effect across an economy.
This introduces burdens and risks after the benefits have been established.
This limits the claim by distinguishing family support from a full development policy.

vocab.inContext: money a worker sends to family or others in another place
the ability to direct resources toward changing needs
exposed to harm when an important source of support fails

skillTips.main-idea: A complete main idea should balance flexible support with the transfer’s costs, risks, and limits.
skillTips.inference: Infer emergency value from who controls the money and how quickly a household can redirect it.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the possible loss of the one supporting job to understand “vulnerable” as exposed to harm.
skillTips.detail: For a reducing factor, distinguish transfer fees from household choices made after funds arrive.

passages.title: What a Deadline Makes Visible
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A deadline is a date and a lamp. Before the date exists, a project can remain pleasantly abstract. Its imagined version contains every possibility and no awkward compromise. Once time becomes limited, choices appear. Which evidence matters? Which feature can wait? Who must answer a question today?

That pressure is useful because attention is finite. A team cannot polish every sentence, explore every path, and still finish. A deadline forces priorities into view. It can also coordinate people who depend on one another. An editor needs a draft before a designer can arrange it; a cook needs the guest count before buying food.

Yet urgency is not proof of importance. An arbitrary date may reward visible speed while hiding exhaustion, skipped testing, or silence from the person who needs more time. Repeated emergencies often signal poor planning rather than heroic commitment. A humane deadline includes enough margin for illness, revision, and discoveries that alter the plan.

The best date is therefore neither infinitely distant nor proudly impossible. It creates a boundary firm enough to prompt decisions and flexible enough to protect the purpose of the work. Sometimes the honest response is to reduce the scope. Sometimes it is to move the date. Those choices are not failures if they make quality and care possible. A deadline makes values visible because something must be protected when everything cannot be. The revealing question is not merely, “Did we finish on time?” It is, “What did our use of time show we were willing to preserve?”

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the essay?
choices: Every deadline should remain fixed even when new evidence changes a project.
Urgent work is always more important than careful work without a date.
A project stays most realistic when no one has to choose among possibilities.
Deadlines reveal priorities and coordinate work, but useful deadlines must protect quality, people, and the project’s real purpose.
questions.explanation: The essay values boundaries while repeatedly qualifying them with humane scope, margin, and purpose.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare a deadline to a lamp?
choices: A time limit exposes choices and priorities that could stay hidden while a project remained abstract.
A deadline supplies physical light for editors and cooks working at night.
A project must use electricity before a designer can arrange it.
A date makes every possible version of a project equally achievable.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says a deadline makes concrete choices appear, like a lamp revealing what was unseen.

questions.stem: What does “margin” mean in the fourth paragraph?
choices: the blank edge around a printed page
extra time or capacity reserved for difficulty and change
profit earned by finishing early
a rule that forbids revision
questions.explanation: The passage says margin accommodates illness, revision, and discoveries, so it is protective extra capacity.

questions.stem: What are two possible responses when a plan cannot meet its current boundary responsibly?
choices: skip testing or silence concerns
add every feature or remove all evidence
reduce the scope or move the date
avoid priorities or keep the project abstract
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph explicitly offers reducing scope and moving the date as honest choices.

lesson.strategy: Track the lamp metaphor through the essay: limits reveal choices, and choices reveal values. Treat each “yet,” “rather than,” and “sometimes” as a guardrail against worshiping speed.

signals.means: This introduces the concrete decisions that an abstract project could postpone.
This blocks the false conclusion that the nearest date marks the greatest value.
This signals a balanced conclusion between an endless project and an impossible demand.

vocab.inContext: existing mainly as an idea without concrete decisions or limits
chosen without a strong reason tied to the project’s purpose
extra time or capacity kept available for problems and revision

skillTips.main-idea: Build the main idea from both functions of deadlines and the safeguards the author says they require.
skillTips.inference: Explain the lamp metaphor by naming what becomes visible only after time is limited.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the list of illness, revision, and discovery to recognize margin as reserved capacity.
skillTips.detail: For a response detail, return to the paired “sometimes” sentences rather than the examples of harmful haste.

passages.title: The Two Clay Cups
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A potter made two clay cups. One cup had a painted blue rim. The other was plain. The painted cup teased its neighbor on the shelf.

“Everyone will choose me,” it said. “You have nothing to show.”

Soon, a traveler bought both cups. At camp, the blue cup held flowers beside the tent. The plain cup carried water to a child, then soup to an elder. By night, its surface bore scratches from use. “You look worse than before,” said the blue cup.

The plain cup answered, “That is true. I also know whose thirst I eased.” The painted cup watched the flowers close in the dark. It no longer mistook being admired for being useful.
