passages.title: Chien-Shiung Wu Tests the Rule
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Chien-Shiung Wu was born in China in 1912. She became an experimental physicist and later worked in the United States. Colleagues respected her skill with difficult measurements.

In the 1950s, physicists wondered whether a rule called parity always held. The rule suggested that some events should behave like their mirror images. Two theorists proposed that weak nuclear interactions might break it. They asked Wu to design a test.

Wu's team cooled radioactive cobalt to an extremely low temperature and aligned its nuclei in a magnetic field. The particles emitted by the cobalt did not leave equally in mirrored directions. The result showed that parity was not conserved in this interaction.

The experiment changed physics. The theorists received a Nobel Prize, while Wu did not share it. Her work remains a clear example of how experimental design can decide between ideas. A bold proposal needed an instrument, controlled conditions, and someone able to make nature answer.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the biography?
choices: Wu won a shared Nobel Prize for proposing parity without testing it.
Chien-Shiung Wu designed a precise cobalt experiment that showed a supposed symmetry rule failed in weak interactions.
Radioactive cobalt emitted particles equally in every mirrored direction.
The parity rule concerned only ordinary mirrors used in laboratories.
questions.explanation: The passage centers Wu’s experimental skill, method, decisive result, and significance.

questions.stem: Why did Wu’s team cool the cobalt and align its nuclei?
choices: They wanted the cobalt to stop being radioactive.
They needed to create a glass mirror around the sample.
They needed controlled conditions that made the two directions meaningfully testable.
They planned to warm the material with emitted particles.
questions.explanation: The apparatus organized the nuclei so an uneven directional pattern could test parity.

questions.stem: What does “conserved” mean here?
choices: placed safely inside a museum
cooled to a low temperature
awarded as a scientific prize
kept unchanged or obeyed in the interaction
questions.explanation: The result showed that the proposed symmetry rule did not remain valid.

questions.stem: What material did Wu’s team study?
choices: radioactive cobalt
liquid water
polished glass
heated iron
questions.explanation: The third paragraph identifies radioactive cobalt as the experimental material.

lesson.strategy: Read proposal and experiment as different contributions. Follow how controlled orientation turns an abstract mirror question into a measurable directional result.

signals.means: This changes parity from an assumed universal rule into a testable question.
This states the observation that contradicted mirrored behavior.
This distinguishes the experiment’s historical importance from how the prize was distributed.

vocab.inContext: a proposed symmetry between a physical event and its mirror image
the dense central parts of atoms
kept valid or unchanged through a physical interaction

skillTips.main-idea: State the main idea around Wu’s experimental test and its result, not only the theorists’ proposal.
skillTips.inference: Infer the apparatus purpose from the need to compare particle emission in organized opposite directions.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use “not” and the broken rule to understand conserved as remaining valid.
skillTips.detail: For the material detail, locate the named substance in the description of the cold apparatus.

passages.title: The Waitlist as a Price Without Money
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A popular free class has twenty seats and sixty interested students. Nobody pays tuition, yet access is still scarce. A waitlist allocates the limited places through time and position instead of through money.

This nonmoney price has consequences. A student must register early, watch messages, and sometimes remain available for a seat that opens suddenly. People with stable schedules and reliable internet may find those tasks easier. A person working unpredictable hours can value the class greatly and still lose a place.

Different rules distribute the burden differently. First-come service rewards speed. A lottery reduces the advantage of arriving first but makes individual outcomes less predictable. Reserved seats can protect access for groups the program is meant to reach. Charging a refundable deposit may discourage casual sign-ups, though even a temporary payment can exclude someone short of cash.

Calling the class free therefore describes its money price, not the full cost of access. Every allocation method asks people to bear something: money, waiting, uncertainty, paperwork, or restricted choice. Good design begins by naming those costs and asking whether they fall on the people the class hopes to serve.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A waitlist proves that any class with no tuition has unlimited space.
First-come registration treats every schedule and internet connection identically.
A free program still allocates scarce access through nonmoney costs, and different rules place those burdens on different people.
A refundable deposit can never exclude a person who lacks cash.
questions.explanation: The passage reveals hidden access costs and compares how allocation methods distribute them.

questions.stem: Why can first-come registration disadvantage some workers?
choices: Workers always value classes less than other students.
First-come rules require everyone to pay tuition.
A lottery reserves every seat for one group.
Unpredictable schedules may make it hard to register quickly or accept a sudden opening.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph connects unstable time with difficulty performing the waitlist tasks.

questions.stem: What does “allocates” mean?
choices: distributes a limited resource among people
makes a class unlimited
removes every access cost
refunds a deposit immediately
questions.explanation: The waitlist and other rules decide who receives scarce seats, so they allocate them.

questions.stem: Which method reduces the advantage of arriving first?
choices: first-come service
a lottery
a sudden opening
a waitlist position
questions.explanation: The third paragraph directly contrasts a lottery with the speed advantage of first-come service.

lesson.strategy: Treat time, attention, uncertainty, and paperwork as real costs even when no money changes hands. Compare each rule by asking who can most easily satisfy its demand.

signals.means: This establishes why a zero money price does not eliminate allocation.
This shifts from one waitlist to comparison among several allocation methods.
This conclusion limits what the word “free” actually tells us.

vocab.inContext: available in a smaller amount than people want
assigns or distributes limited places among people
money paid temporarily and returned if stated conditions are met

skillTips.main-idea: A complete main idea names hidden nonmoney costs and their unequal distribution.
skillTips.inference: Infer the worker’s disadvantage from the timing tasks required to keep a waitlist place.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use all the rules that decide who gets seats to define allocates as distributes.
skillTips.detail: For the speed comparison, return to the sentences contrasting first-come service and a lottery.

passages.title: The Discipline of Returning
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Beginning receives more ceremony than returning. A new notebook looks clean; a first run feels decisive. Returning on the seventh rainy morning rarely receives applause. Yet most practices are built in that ordinary second movement: not starting once, but coming back after novelty has left.

Return should not be confused with perfect consistency. Illness interrupts, care for others rearranges time, and discouragement can make a week disappear. If one missed day becomes proof of failure, a small break grows into abandonment. A durable practice needs a way back.

That way can be modest. Open the instrument case and play one scale. Read one page. Put on walking shoes and travel to the corner. A deliberately small action lowers the drama of restarting. It also preserves identity: this is still something I do, even if today's version is brief.

There is no virtue in returning to every goal forever. A practice may be harmful, no longer possible, or tied to a self one has thoughtfully outgrown. Discipline includes evaluation. The question is whether resistance comes from a genuine change in value or from the ordinary discomfort of beginning again. Returning matters because a life will contain interruption. The skill is not arranging a flawless chain of days. It is learning which commitments deserve another approach and making the next step small enough to take.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the essay?
choices: A worthy practice requires an unbroken chain with no missed days.
Every old goal should be continued forever regardless of harm or changed values.
Only dramatic restarts can preserve a person’s sense of identity.
Durable practice depends on returning after interruption through manageable steps, while still reevaluating whether a commitment deserves continuation.
questions.explanation: The essay joins gentle reentry with thoughtful judgment about which practices remain worth pursuing.

questions.stem: Why does the author recommend one scale or one page?
choices: A small action reduces the difficulty of restarting and reconnects a person with the practice.
A brief action guarantees that no future interruption will occur.
Small actions make evaluation of goals unnecessary.
One page creates more ceremony than a new notebook.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph links modest steps with lower drama and preserved identity.

questions.stem: What does “durable” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: performed perfectly every day
able to continue through strain and interruption
new enough to feel exciting
finished in a single attempt
questions.explanation: A durable practice includes a way back after missed time, so it can survive disruption.

questions.stem: What two possible sources of resistance does the essay compare?
choices: illness and a clean notebook
applause and a first run
a genuine change in value and the discomfort of restarting
one scale and one page
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph poses that exact evaluation between changed values and ordinary restart discomfort.

lesson.strategy: Notice how the essay redefines discipline twice: first as return rather than perfection, then as evaluation rather than endless repetition. The small-step examples connect these ideas to action.

signals.means: This turns attention from celebrated beginnings to the less visible work of continuing.
This separates returning from an impossible standard of perfect consistency.
This qualifies persistence by making room for thoughtful endings.

vocab.inContext: the energizing quality of being new
able to remain viable despite interruption or difficulty
leaving a practice behind completely

skillTips.main-idea: Include manageable return and honest reevaluation in the main idea; either alone misses the balance.
skillTips.inference: Infer the value of tiny actions from how they lower restart drama and preserve identity.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the practice’s “way back” after disruption to define durable as able to continue.
skillTips.detail: For the final comparison, locate the two explanations for resistance posed in paragraph four.

passages.title: The Raven's Bright Button
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A raven found a silver button beside the road. It flashed when he tilted it toward the sun. He carried it to the tallest pine and announced that the sky had given him a piece of morning. The magpie admired the shine. The mole asked whether it could mend a coat. The raven tucked the button beneath one wing. “Its purpose is higher than coats,” he said.

Each day he polished it. Because one wing stayed pressed around the treasure, his flight became uneven. He stopped carrying twigs for the nest he shared with his sister. He avoided rain, fearing spots. When the flock searched a field, he watched from a dry branch and guarded his brightness.

Then winter ice sealed the berries beneath a hard crust. The raven's sister tried to lift it with her beak, but the layer would not break. The mole knew of grain inside an abandoned shed. Its door was fastened by a loop of wire whose ends almost met. “A small round object might hold them together,” said the mole. The raven imagined his button scratched inside the loop. He also saw his sister's empty beak. At last he fitted the button through the wire. The door opened, and the flock ate. The silver surface gained a deep mark.

In spring, the raven still kept the button, but he wore it on a cord where everyone could see the scratch. “Is that damage?” a nestling asked. “It is the first thing this treasure ever accomplished,” said the raven.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the fable?
choices: The raven learns that a treasured object gains deeper value through useful sacrifice rather than untouched display.
A silver button is valuable only while its surface remains perfectly polished.
The mole steals the raven’s treasure and uses it to decorate a shed.
The raven’s sister refuses to eat food reached with a scratched object.
questions.explanation: The button’s mark becomes evidence of helping the flock, reversing the raven’s original idea of value.

questions.stem: Why does the raven later display the scratch?
choices: He wants the flock to believe the button is newly found.
He now sees it as a record of the button’s useful service to others.
The scratch makes the silver flash more brightly.
He is warning nestlings never to enter the shed.
questions.explanation: His answer calls the mark an accomplishment rather than damage.

questions.stem: What does “fastened” mean in the fourth paragraph?
choices: covered by winter berries
polished until it shines
held closed or joined securely
carried beneath a wing
questions.explanation: The loop of wire keeps the shed door closed until the button joins its ends.

questions.stem: What is stored inside the abandoned shed?
choices: berries
silver buttons
pine twigs
grain
questions.explanation: The mole tells the hungry birds about grain inside the shed.

lesson.strategy: Track what the button costs the raven before it is used and what the scratch means afterward. The same mark changes from feared damage into evidence of contribution.

signals.means: This reveals the raven’s empty claim that display is superior to ordinary usefulness.
This places his fear of damage beside his sister’s immediate need.
This contrast shows he keeps the object while changing how he values it.

vocab.inContext: rubbed until a surface becomes smooth and bright
held shut or joined securely
successfully achieved something of value

skillTips.main-idea: State the lesson through the button’s changed meaning, not simply through the flock finding food.
skillTips.inference: Infer why the raven displays the scratch from his final explanation of what the button achieved.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the wire loop holding the door to define fastened as secured closed.
skillTips.detail: For the stored food, return to the mole’s knowledge before the group reaches the shed.

passages.title: The Door You Chose to Close
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Every choice closes some doors. Joining the school play may mean missing a game. Saving money for a bicycle may mean skipping a treat. This can make a good choice feel like a loss. The limit gives the choice weight.

A closed door does not prove the choice was wrong. Choice matters because we cannot do everything at once. Giving time to one path helps that path become real.

Still, some choices can be changed. A student may join the next game, or choose a different goal for the savings. Wisdom means knowing which doors are truly locked and which can open later. It also means accepting that a meaningful yes often includes a real no.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A good choice lets a person do every possible activity at once.
Meaningful choices require giving up alternatives, though some closed paths can be reopened later.
Feeling a loss proves that a decision was wrong.
Every closed door remains locked forever.
questions.explanation: The passage explains tradeoffs while distinguishing permanent choices from changeable ones.

questions.stem: Why can a good choice still feel like a loss?
choices: A good choice never helps anything become real.
All games and plays happen on different days.
Choosing one path means giving up another possibility for now.
Saving money removes the bicycle goal.
questions.explanation: The opening examples show one valued option being sacrificed for another.

questions.stem: What does “path” mean here?
choices: a paved road beside a school
a locked wooden door
money saved in a jar
a course of action or possibility
questions.explanation: The path is something a choice gives time to and makes real.

questions.stem: What might saving for a bicycle require skipping?
choices: a treat
a school play
the next game
a different door
questions.explanation: The first paragraph pairs bicycle savings with skipping a treat.

lesson.strategy: Read doors and paths as metaphors for options. The final paragraph adds an important distinction between a temporary sacrifice and an irreversible choice.

signals.means: This blocks the conclusion that regret automatically signals a mistake.
This qualifies the image of permanently closed doors.
This connects commitment to the alternative that must be refused.

vocab.inContext: a decision between available possibilities
a possible direction for action or life
recognizing a reality without pretending it is absent

skillTips.main-idea: The main idea should include both real tradeoffs and the possibility of later change.
skillTips.inference: Infer the feeling of loss from the valued option left behind when one path is chosen.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the figurative doors around it to read path as an option rather than a road.
skillTips.detail: For the savings example, return to the paired choices in the opening paragraph.

passages.title: When Work Makes the Clock Disappear
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A painter looks up and discovers that two hours have passed. A climber moves from hold to hold without thinking about lunch. This deep involvement is often called flow.

Flow is more likely when a task is challenging but manageable. The person knows the goal and receives clear feedback. Each brushstroke changes the picture; each movement changes the climber's position. Attention stays with the next useful action.

If a task is far too easy, boredom may enter. If it feels impossible, worry can crowd out concentration. Skill and challenge need a workable match. Flow also cannot justify ignoring every signal from the body or every duty to others.

Losing track of time is one sign, not the whole definition. Flow combines focused attention, action, and a sense of progress. It is not magic and cannot be ordered on command. People can only shape conditions that make it more likely.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Flow occurs whenever a task is either effortless or completely impossible.
Losing track of time excuses ignoring health and other people.
Flow is deep task involvement encouraged by matched challenge, clear goals, feedback, and focused progress.
A person can command flow to begin instantly in any setting.
questions.explanation: The passage defines flow, describes supportive conditions, and sets limits on the idea.

questions.stem: Why does immediate feedback support flow?
choices: It makes the task impossible to complete.
It removes the need for attention.
It guarantees a person will skip lunch.
It shows how each action changes progress toward the goal.
questions.explanation: The painter and climber can see what each next action accomplishes.

questions.stem: What does “manageable” mean?
choices: difficult but possible to handle
so easy that boredom appears
unrelated to a clear goal
too difficult to attempt
questions.explanation: The task must challenge skill without feeling impossible, so manageable means handleable.

questions.stem: What feeling may appear when a task is too easy?
choices: worry
boredom
hunger
surprise
questions.explanation: The third paragraph directly links excessive ease with boredom.

lesson.strategy: Compare the task with the person’s current skill, then locate the goal and feedback loop. Treat time loss as evidence of flow, not its complete definition.

signals.means: This sets the useful middle ground between boredom and impossible challenge.
These paired conditions show what happens when the skill-challenge match fails.
This prevents one vivid symptom from replacing the fuller concept.

vocab.inContext: a state of deep, organized involvement in an activity
information showing the result of an action
possible to handle despite requiring effort

skillTips.main-idea: Include both the experience of flow and the conditions that make it more likely.
skillTips.inference: Infer feedback’s role from how each action visibly changes the task.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the contrast with impossible challenge to define manageable as possible to handle.
skillTips.detail: For the easy-task detail, locate the paired outcomes of boredom and worry.

passages.title: The Language Between Machines
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Two computers can share a cable and still fail to communicate. A path is not enough. They need shared rules for formatting messages, identifying senders and receivers, and responding when information is lost. Such a rule set is called a protocol.

Consider mailing a package. An address follows an expected order. A label states where the package should go, while systems along the route decide the next step. The receiver can check whether the contents arrived intact. Network protocols divide digital information into packets and attach similar routing and checking information.

Different protocols solve different parts of communication. One may move packets reliably between programs. Another may define how a browser requests a web page. Layers allow engineers to replace one technology without redesigning everything above it. A wireless link and a fiber cable can carry the same higher-level request in different ways.

Shared rules do not require identical machines. That is their strength. A phone, server, and home router may be built by different companies, yet each can participate if it follows the relevant protocol. The useful “language” between machines is therefore less like a rich human conversation and more like a precise agreement about structure, sequence, and response.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A physical cable guarantees that two computers understand every message.
All network tasks are controlled by one rule that cannot be replaced.
Protocols require phones, routers, and servers to be built by one company.
Protocols let different machines exchange information by following precise shared rules at several communication layers.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the need, analogy, layered roles, and interoperability created by protocols.

questions.stem: Why are protocol layers useful?
choices: One communication technology can change without forcing every higher function to be redesigned.
They make addresses and error checks unnecessary.
They require wireless links to become fiber cables.
They combine every network role into one machine.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph explicitly connects layers with replacing one technology independently.

questions.stem: What does “protocol” mean in this passage?
choices: a cable joining two identical computers
an agreed set of rules for exchanging information
one piece of a mailed package
a company that builds routers
questions.explanation: The opening defines a protocol as shared rules for message format, addressing, and response.

questions.stem: What digital units can carry routing and checking information?
choices: browsers
companies
packets
fibers
questions.explanation: The package analogy leads to packets with attached routing and checking information.

lesson.strategy: Use the package analogy to identify distinct jobs without treating it as an exact match. Then follow how layered rules create cooperation among unlike devices.

signals.means: This establishes that connection alone does not supply shared meaning.
This divides communication into specialized layers and tasks.
This points to interoperability rather than identical construction as the benefit.

vocab.inContext: an agreed set of structures and responses for communication
small organized units into which network information is divided
choosing paths that move information toward its destination

skillTips.main-idea: State the main idea around shared rules, layered jobs, and communication among different machines.
skillTips.inference: Infer the value of layering from the wireless and fiber example of interchangeable lower technology.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the explicit opening definition to select the rule-set meaning of protocol.
skillTips.detail: For the digital unit, trace the comparison immediately after the mailed package description.

passages.title: A House Full of Clocks
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
When Aunt Sela left Mara the narrow blue house, every room contained a clock. A kitchen clock chimed; a painted bird jumped from another. Travel clocks crowded a shelf. Mara planned to sell them. Their ticking made sleep feel like waiting. Then she found a note beneath it: “This one ran fast when your mother missed the train.” Other notes recalled repairs, a blackout, and shared soup.

The notes did not make the clocks valuable antiques. Most were common and several were broken. They did something stranger: they turned incorrect time into precise memory. Mara spent Saturday matching notes with objects. She heard Aunt Sela’s voice in the brisk descriptions but found no instruction to keep anything.

On Sunday, the dealer named a modest price for the whole collection. Mara sold most of it. She kept the kitchen clock, even though it gained seven minutes each day, and gave the painted bird to her brother. Then she placed the notes in a plain box.

That night the house was nearly quiet. Mara missed the layered ticking, but she also heard rain at the window. She understood that preserving a life did not require preserving every object it had touched. Memory needed a few doors, not a warehouse. The fast clock chimed early, and Mara smiled without correcting it.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the story?
choices: Mara learns to preserve selected objects and stories without keeping every clock connected to her aunt’s life.
Mara discovers that all her aunt’s common clocks are extremely valuable antiques.
The dealer refuses to buy any clock because their times do not match.
Accurate time matters more to Mara than the memories recorded in the notes.
questions.explanation: Her final choices balance release with preservation rather than treating the collection as all or nothing.

questions.stem: Why does Mara keep the inaccurate kitchen clock?
choices: It is the only antique worth a large amount of money.
Its note connects the clock with a meaningful family memory.
The dealer orders her to correct it every day.
Its early chime makes every train arrive on time.
questions.explanation: She keeps it after learning the story about her mother and the missed train.

questions.stem: What does “modest” mean when describing the dealer’s price?
choices: secret and unspoken
exactly seven minutes late
not especially large
greater than every antique value
questions.explanation: The clocks are common and broken, so the offered price is limited rather than high.

questions.stem: What does Mara give her brother?
choices: the plain box of notes
the blue house
the brass kitchen clock
the clock with the painted bird
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says she gives the painted-bird clock to her brother.

lesson.strategy: Track Mara’s movement from selling everything to making selective choices. The notes alter what the clocks mean without issuing a command or turning them into costly antiques.

signals.means: This shifts value from money and accuracy to the memories attached to objects.
This preserves Mara’s responsibility to choose rather than obey the past.
This states the balanced understanding behind her final decisions.

vocab.inContext: made a ringing sound to mark a time
limited in amount rather than unusually large
keeping something available instead of letting it be lost

skillTips.main-idea: Make the main idea reflect Mara’s selective preservation, not a total rejection or total keeping.
skillTips.inference: Infer the kitchen clock’s value from the memory written specifically beneath it.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the clocks’ common condition and the collection sale to define modest as not large.
skillTips.detail: For the gift detail, distinguish the clock Mara keeps from the different one she gives away.

passages.title: The Māori Parliament at Waipatu
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In June 1892, Māori leaders and representatives gathered at Waipatu in Hawke's Bay, New Zealand. The meeting became the first session of Te Kotahitanga, the Māori Parliament. Its members sought ways to address land loss, laws imposed without Māori influence, and the relationship between Māori authority and the colonial government.

Te Kotahitanga drew on traditions of hui, or deliberative gatherings, while adopting parliamentary forms such as elected representation, debates, committees, and recorded proceedings. Women participated in the movement and pressed for political voice. Meri Te Tai Mangakāhia addressed the parliament in 1893 and argued that women should be able to vote and stand for membership.

The organization did not remain in one permanent building. Sessions met at several Māori communities, and local hosts provided food, shelter, and meeting space. Movement made the parliament a national network, but travel and funding were difficult. Delegates also brought different tribal priorities, so unity required negotiation rather than simple agreement. Te Kotahitanga petitioned the Crown and debated proposals for authority over Māori affairs. The colonial government did not recognize it as a separate governing parliament. That refusal limited its formal power, while disagreement about strategy also shaped its course. Sessions continued until 1902.

Judging the movement only by the laws it could enforce would miss its importance. At Waipatu and later meetings, participants practiced representative debate, documented shared concerns, and asserted that decisions affecting Māori should not be made without Māori political agency. Te Kotahitanga was both an institution with constraints and an enduring claim to collective voice.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The colonial government immediately recognized Te Kotahitanga as New Zealand’s only parliament.
Te Kotahitanga created a Māori representative forum for collective political voice despite limited recognition, resources, and internal differences.
Te Kotahitanga stayed permanently at Waipatu and avoided participation by women.
All Māori representatives entered the movement with identical tribal priorities and strategies.
questions.explanation: The passage presents its practices, claims, obstacles, and significance without reducing it to formal legal power.

questions.stem: Why did sessions meet in several communities?
choices: The Crown required every debate to occur in a different country.
Delegates refused all food and shelter at Waipatu.
Te Kotahitanga functioned as a wider network without one permanent parliamentary building.
A fixed building would have granted automatic governing power.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph explains both the moving sessions and their national, locally hosted character.

questions.stem: What does “agency” mean in the final paragraph?
choices: a building used for one parliamentary session
complete agreement among every tribe
a petition automatically made into law
the capacity to participate in and shape political decisions
questions.explanation: The phrase demands Māori involvement in decisions affecting Māori, so agency means power to act and influence.

questions.stem: Who argued in 1893 that women should vote and stand for membership?
choices: Meri Te Tai Mangakāhia
Robert Paine
Piri Reis
Chien-Shiung Wu
questions.explanation: The second paragraph names Meri Te Tai Mangakāhia and summarizes her argument.

lesson.strategy: Read institutional form, practical limits, and political claim together. The final paragraph asks readers to measure influence through participation and asserted authority, not only enforceable laws.

signals.means: This connects Māori traditions of gathering with selected parliamentary procedures.
This qualifies the benefit of a mobile national network with its practical costs.
This redirects evaluation from formal enforcement to political practice and voice.

vocab.inContext: a Māori gathering for meeting, discussion, or deliberation
people chosen to represent communities in a larger meeting
the capacity to act and influence decisions

skillTips.main-idea: Include representative practice, collective voice, and limits on recognition in the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Infer the moving sessions’ network role from local hosting and the lack of one permanent building.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the demand for involvement in decisions to define agency as capacity to shape them.
skillTips.detail: For the women’s political-rights detail, return to the named 1893 address in paragraph two.

passages.title: The Dandelion's Flying Seed
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A dandelion seed hangs beneath a white crown of fine hairs. The crown is called a pappus. When wind pulls the seed free, the hairs spread wide.

The pappus does not flap like a bird's wing. Air moves through and around its many hairs. This creates a swirling pocket above the seed and slows its fall. A light seed can then stay in the air longer.

Most seeds land near the parent plant. Some meet a useful gust and travel much farther. Flying does not promise success. A seed still needs a place with light, water, and soil. The pappus simply gives chance and wind more time to carry it somewhere new across open ground.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A dandelion seed flies by flapping its hairs like bird wings.
Every dandelion seed travels far from its parent.
A dandelion’s pappus slows its falling seed, giving wind more time to carry it.
Wind guarantees that a seed will find water and soil.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the structure, the air effect, and the limited opportunity it creates.

questions.stem: Why can a light seed travel farther?
choices: Its pappus becomes a heavy wing.
It always lands beside its parent.
It no longer needs soil or water.
Its slow fall leaves more time for wind to move it.
questions.explanation: The second and third paragraphs connect longer air time with wind transport.

questions.stem: What is a “pappus”?
choices: the crown of fine hairs above the seed
the root beneath a mature plant

passages.title: What a Stage Manager Calls
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
During a theater performance, actors speak the lines, but a stage manager coordinates the event. From a desk or booth, the manager follows a marked script and listens to communication from the crew.

The script contains cues. A cue is the agreed moment for an action: lights fade after a word, music begins on a gesture, or a curtain moves when a scene ends. The stage manager warns the correct operator to get ready, then calls “go” at the exact moment.

Calling cues requires attention to the live performance. An actor may pause longer than usual, or a piece of scenery may move slowly. The manager cannot depend only on a stopwatch. The call must follow what is actually happening while keeping many departments together.

Rehearsals let the team practice this sequence and solve risks before an audience arrives. A calm voice on the headset may be unheard by the crowd, yet it helps turn separate actions into one repeatable show.

passages.title: When Earth Hides the Moon
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth moves between the Sun and the full Moon. The Moon passes into Earth's shadow. This alignment does not happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted compared with Earth's path around the Sun.

Earth's shadow has a lighter outer region called the penumbra and a darker central region called the umbra. If only part of the Moon enters the umbra, observers see a partial eclipse. If the whole Moon enters it, the eclipse is total.

During totality, the Moon often looks red or copper instead of disappearing. Sunlight passes through Earth's atmosphere before reaching the shadowed Moon. The atmosphere scatters much of the shorter blue light and bends some red light inward. Dust and clouds can change the exact color and darkness.

People on Earth's night side can watch a lunar eclipse without special eye protection. Unlike a solar eclipse, it does not require looking toward the bright Sun. The event makes a large geometry visible: the curved edge of Earth's shadow crosses the Moon while filtered sunlight colors the darkness.

passages.title: Edmonia Lewis Carves Her Own Path
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Edmonia Lewis was the first widely recognized sculptor of African American and Native American heritage. Born around 1844, she studied at Oberlin College, which admitted women and Black students. Racism and violence disrupted her education, but she continued creating. Lewis moved to Boston, where abolitionists supported her work. She sold portrait medallions of antislavery figures and traveled to Rome in 1865. Rome offered an international community and access to marble and classical sculpture.

Many sculptors designed works and hired Italian artisans to transfer it into marble. Lewis often emphasized carving her own stone. She knew viewers might otherwise deny her skill and credit the workshop. The choice demanded intense labor, yet it asserted authorship in a field shaped by racism and sexism.

Her sculptures drew on biblical stories, freedom, and Native American subjects. “Forever Free,” made after the end of slavery in the United States, presents a Black couple at emancipation. Her large work “The Death of Cleopatra” impressed viewers at the 1876 Centennial Exhibition, then disappeared from the art world for decades before being recovered and restored.

Lewis shaped both marble and the conditions under which people saw her. She worked within popular styles while choosing subjects tied to identity and liberation. Her path shows that artistic authorship includes not only imagining a form, but securing the right to be recognized as its maker.

passages.title: The Same Basket in Two Countries
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Suppose a basket of rice, rent, transit, soap, and medicine costs 100 currency units in one country and 200 in another. A market rate may exchange the first 100 for 150 of the second. That conversion would not fully reflect local purchasing power. Economists use purchasing power parity, or PPP, to compare what money can buy within different economies. They price a broad basket of goods and services, then estimate a conversion rate that gives the basket similar value in each place. PPP-adjusted income often differs from income converted at financial-market rates.

The method answers an important question, but constructing the “same” basket is difficult. Foods, housing, public services, and habits differ. A train trip in a dense city may not be equivalent to fuel in a rural area. Quality changes, informal markets, and missing price data add uncertainty. National averages can also hide sharp regional and household differences.

Market rates still matter for imported goods, foreign debt, travel, and trade. PPP is more useful for some comparisons of living standards or the size of economies. Neither rate is the single true value of a currency; each is designed for a different question.

A good comparison therefore begins by naming its purpose. If the question is how much food and shelter local wages support, relative local prices matter. If the question is how many imported machines a company can purchase, the market rate may matter more. The basket is a model, not a universal shopping list, but it makes hidden price differences visible.

passages.title: The Unfinished Shelf
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An unfinished shelf leaned against my wall for months. Its boards were cut, but one bracket was missing. Each day, I noticed the gap and thought, “I should finish that.”

The shelf took no action, yet it used a little attention. I pictured the tool I needed and the books still on the floor. Small unfinished tasks can stay open in the mind like quiet questions.

One Saturday, I wrote down two choices: buy the bracket or give away the boards. The list felt kinder than another promise. I bought the part and finished the shelf.

Not every task must be completed. Some should be released. The relief came from making a decision, not only from driving the final screw.

passages.title: The Snail's Painted Shell
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A snail envied the butterflies above the garden. Their wings carried orange spots and blue bands. His shell looked like a brown stone.

He asked a child to paint it. Soon, yellow stars and green leaves covered every curve. The snail thanked the child and began his slow trip home.

Rain fell. The paint became sticky. Dry petals clung to the shell, then twigs, then a crumpled seed case. The extra load made each step harder. When the snail reached a puddle, he washed until most colors drifted away. A butterfly landed nearby. “I am sorry you lost your decoration,” she said.

The snail looked at the pale swirls that remained. “I wanted your beauty without asking how your wings carried it,” he replied. After that, he still enjoyed bright colors, but he admired them without turning every difference into a lack.

passages.title: Is a Kind Lie Still a Lie?
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A friend shows you a painting and asks whether it is good. You see serious problems, but you also see their nervous hope. Saying “It is perfect” may protect them for a moment. It may also deny them information they need.

The conflict is not simply truth against kindness. A truthful answer can be cruel if it aims to embarrass. A gentle answer can remain honest: “The colors hold my attention, but I lose the subject near the center.” Timing matters too. Someone asking for comfort after a painful day may need a different response from someone requesting critique before an exhibition.

A kind lie still involves knowingly leading another person away from what one believes. That gives it a moral cost. Yet truthfulness does not require reporting every thought without care or permission. We choose what to say, how precisely to say it, and whether we are the right person to say it.

The better question may be what the relationship asks of us at that moment. Respect includes concern for another person's feelings and concern for their ability to make informed choices. Kindness and honesty become rivals only when imagination fails to find language that takes both seriously.

passages.title: The Strange Feeling of Having Been Here
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In an unfamiliar café, you suddenly feel this moment has happened before. The conviction is vivid, yet no earlier visit emerges. This mismatch is déjà vu, French for “already seen.” Déjà vu is common, especially among younger adults, and usually lasts only seconds. It is not itself proof of a hidden memory, prediction, or supernatural event. Researchers instead study how systems for familiarity and detailed recollection may briefly separate.

Familiarity is the general signal that something has been encountered. Recollection supplies context: where, when, and with whom. Normally those processes support each other. During déjà vu, a new scene may trigger a strong familiarity signal without the details that would identify a real past episode.

Why might that happen? A current layout may resemble an earlier place that is not consciously recalled. Attention may register part of a scene before the rest, making the completed perception feel repeated. Researchers have proposed several mechanisms, and no single explanation covers every case.

The feeling is interesting precisely because certainty and evidence pull apart. A person can acknowledge the experience without treating its message as fact. Frequent déjà vu accompanied by confusion or other symptoms deserves medical attention, but an occasional passing episode is generally an ordinary feature of memory. It reveals that feeling familiar and retrieving a source are related achievements, not the same one.

passages.title: The Satellite That Watches Crops
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A crop satellite does not see a field as a farmer does. Its sensors measure energy reflected or emitted from patches of Earth's surface. Different wavelength bands reveal different features, including color, near-infrared reflection, surface temperature, and moisture-related signals. Healthy leaves absorb much visible red light for photosynthesis while reflecting strongly in near-infrared wavelengths. Analysts combine those measurements into vegetation indices. Repeated images can show where plant cover is changing faster or slower than expected. Thermal observations may reveal unusually warm areas associated with water stress.

The signal is not a diagnosis by itself. Bare soil, crop type, growth stage, clouds, smoke, viewing angle, and sensor resolution can alter the pattern. One image may mix several conditions inside a single pixel. A farmer or adviser compares satellite evidence with weather, planting records, field visits, and knowledge of local soil.

Orbit creates both reach and delay. A satellite can observe large or remote areas with the same instrument, supporting regional drought assessment and planning. Yet it passes on a schedule, and clouds can hide the ground when a decision is urgent. Aircraft, drones, and field sensors can supply closer or more frequent observations at smaller scales.

Useful monitoring therefore connects scales. A broad image identifies an unusual patch; a person investigates its cause; later images show whether the condition spreads or improves. The satellite does not replace local judgment. It makes patterns visible that are difficult to see while standing among individual plants, then returns those patterns to people who can interpret and act on them.

Each morning, Mr. Arun sat on the bench beneath the fig tree. Lila passed him on her walk to school. They waved but never spoke.

One Monday, the bench was empty. A small paper bag rested there. Inside were three ripe figs and a note: “Please share these. My knee needs rest.”

Lila gave one fig to the crossing guard and one to a new student. She saved the last for Mr. Arun. After school, she knocked on his door.

On Friday, Mr. Arun returned to the bench with a cane. Lila sat beside him. The empty place had taught her that a daily wave was already a small friendship. A bag of figs gave them the reason to say it aloud.

choices: Sharing figs helps Lila recognize and deepen a quiet everyday friendship with Arun.
Lila keeps every fig because she does not know anyone nearby.
Mr. Arun leaves the bench because the fig tree has been removed.
The crossing guard writes a note asking for a cane.
questions.explanation: The absence, shared fruit, visit, and final conversation turn a routine greeting into acknowledged friendship.

She wants to return kindness to Mr. Arun when she visits him.
She plans to plant a new tree at school.

lesson.strategy: Notice how absence changes the meaning of a repeated wave. Follow each fig to see how sharing expands the quiet connection.

passages.title: The Temples Moved to Higher Ground
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In the 1960s, a new dam on the Nile threatened the ancient temples at Abu Simbel in Egypt. The planned reservoir would cover their original site with water. The dams also forced many Nubian families to leave towns and villages that the rising water would submerge.

Egypt and Sudan asked for international help. Engineers and workers cut the temples into more than one thousand stone blocks. Many blocks weighed about thirty tons. Each piece was marked so it could return to the correct position.

The team rebuilt the temples on higher ground, about sixty-four meters above the old site and farther inland. An artificial hill helped reproduce the original setting. The work was completed in 1968.

The rescue did not move a whole mountain in one piece. It combined archaeology, engineering, funding, and cooperation across countries. The rebuilt site preserved the great carved figures and interior spaces while the reservoir formed below. Its survival changed what large projects attempted.

choices: The Abu Simbel temples floated uphill in one unbroken piece.
An international project rebuilt Abu Simbel above a new reservoir, whose dams also displaced Nubian communities.
A reservoir was drained permanently so the original site stayed dry.
Workers replaced the ancient carvings with modern copies.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the reservoir’s human cost as well as the block-by-block temple rescue and cooperation.

questions.stem: Why was each stone block marked?
choices: So the block would weigh less than thirty tons.
So the reservoir could form inside it.
So workers could rebuild it in the correct position.
So the original temple would disappear.
questions.explanation: Marking preserved the placement information needed after cutting the structure apart.

questions.stem: What does “reservoir” mean?
choices: a carved figure inside a temple
a machine for cutting stone
a group of countries
a large stored body of water
questions.explanation: The dam’s reservoir would cover the old site with water.

questions.stem: When was the relocation work completed?
questions.explanation: The third paragraph gives 1968 as the completion year.

lesson.strategy: Read the rescue as a sequence: water threat, displacement, numbered pieces, and higher reconstruction. Keep the engineering achievement beside the human cost.

signals.means: This states the danger created by the planned body of water.
This explains the practical purpose of marking each cut block.
This corrects the image of transporting the entire site intact.

skillTips.main-idea: Include the reservoir’s human cost as well as the block-by-block rebuilding method.
skillTips.inference: Infer the reason for markings from the need to restore each piece to its location.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the dam and covering water to define reservoir.
skillTips.detail: For the date, return to the completed reconstruction in the third paragraph.

passages.title: The Moonflower and Its Night Visitor
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
As evening cools, a moonflower opens a pale, trumpet-shaped bloom. Its strong scent spreads through the dark. These features attract night-flying visitors, including large moths that can reach nectar deep inside the flower.

A moth approaches by following odor and visual contrast. It hovers near the bloom and unrolls a long feeding tube called a proboscis. As the moth drinks, its head or body brushes the flower's pollen. At another bloom, some pollen may touch the receptive surface that enables fertilization.

The exchange is useful to both organisms, but it is not a promise between them. The moth seeks food; the flower's traits make pollen transfer more likely. A visitor may take nectar without carrying useful pollen, and weather can keep moths away.

Moonflowers also have a limited schedule. Individual blooms often open for one night and close after morning arrives. Timing scent, pale color, nectar, and flower shape around nocturnal animals concentrates the plant's effort. The partnership is therefore built from matching opportunities: a moth active in darkness meets a flower briefly ready to receive and give.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Moonflowers make binding promises with every moth that drinks nectar.
A moth carries pollen by wrapping it inside its proboscis.
Moonflowers use nighttime scent, color, shape, and timing to increase pollen transfer by visiting moths.
Each moonflower stays open through many weeks of daylight.
questions.explanation: The passage links coordinated flower traits with moth behavior while noting the interaction is not guaranteed.

questions.stem: Why is the flower pale and strongly scented?
choices: They keep all moths from approaching nectar.
They allow the flower to remain open for weeks.
They guarantee every visitor carries pollen.
Those traits help nocturnal visitors locate it in darkness.
questions.explanation: The opening and conclusion connect visual contrast and scent with night-active animals.

questions.stem: What is a “proboscis”?
choices: a moth’s long feeding tube
the flower’s pollen surface
a pale petal
a morning wind
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly names the unrolled feeding tube as a proboscis.

questions.stem: How long does an individual bloom often remain open?
choices: for an entire year
for one night
only at noon
until every moth visits
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says individual blooms often open for one night.

lesson.strategy: Follow the matching traits on both sides: a night-active moth and a briefly open, scented flower. Keep increased probability separate from guaranteed exchange.

signals.means: This connects feeding behavior with accidental contact that moves pollen.

signals.phrase: but it is not a promise
signals.means: This qualifies the mutual benefit by rejecting intention or guaranteed success.
This conclusion gathers the timing and trait matches into one relationship.

skillTips.inference: Infer the pale color and scent functions from the visitor’s limited nighttime conditions.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the direct naming sentence to identify a proboscis as the moth’s feeding tube.
skillTips.detail: For bloom duration, separate one flower’s short opening from the plant’s longer life.

passages.title: What a Cooper Builds
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A cooper makes wooden vessels such as barrels, casks, buckets, and tubs. A barrel is not carved from one block. It is assembled from narrow boards called staves, held in a curved arrangement by hoops. The cooper selects straight-grained wood and shapes each stave so its edges meet its neighbors. The boards are wider in the middle, giving the finished vessel its bulging form. Their angles must be precise. A gap can allow liquid to escape.

To bend the staves, the cooper may heat or steam them, then draw their ends together with temporary hoops. Permanent metal or wooden hoops compress the assembled wall. A circular groove cut inside the ends receives the flat head pieces. When wood swells slightly with moisture, joints can tighten further.

Different contents require different choices. Some beverages gain flavor from oak during storage. A dry-goods barrel may emphasize strength and low weight. Containers intended for liquids demand especially tight construction. Repairs matter too: a skilled cooper can replace a damaged stave or hoop instead of discarding the vessel.

The craft uses geometry without hiding it. Every board remains visible, yet many angled surfaces create one round, strong container. No glue is necessary in many traditional barrels. Shape, wood movement, and hoop tension keep the parts cooperating. A cooper therefore builds both an object and a balanced system of forces.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: A traditional barrel is carved whole from a single block and held only by glue.
Every barrel uses identical wood and construction regardless of what it stores.
A damaged stave requires the entire vessel to be discarded.
A cooper shapes and joins staves, hoops, and heads so geometry, moisture, and compression create a strong vessel.
questions.explanation: The passage explains components, process, content-based choices, repair, and the forces holding a barrel together.

questions.stem: Why are stave edges shaped precisely?
choices: Close-fitting edges help prevent gaps that could leak.
Wide gaps make the hoops compress more strongly.
The vessel must remain flat instead of curved.
Precise edges remove the need for a head.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph directly connects meeting edges and leakage.

questions.stem: What are “staves”?
choices: the circular pieces closing both ends
the narrow shaped boards forming a barrel’s sides
the grooves cut into a workshop floor
the beverages aged inside oak
questions.explanation: The opening defines staves, and later paragraphs describe bending and joining them.

questions.stem: What helps bend the staves?
choices: dry grain alone
removing every hoop
heat or steam
cutting one solid block
questions.explanation: The second paragraph names heat or steam before the ends are drawn together.

lesson.strategy: Build the vessel from named components and forces. Track what each part does, then connect precision, swelling, and compression with the absence of glue.

signals.means: This corrects the misconception that a barrel begins as one hollowed piece.
This introduces design choices based on the vessel’s intended use.
This points to visible boards forming a unified geometric structure.

skillTips.inference: Infer why precision matters by imagining what liquid does at an open seam.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the direct opening definition and later bending process to identify staves.
skillTips.detail: For the bending method, locate what happens before temporary hoops pull the ends together.

passages.title: The Tunnel Through a Barrier
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A low-energy ball cannot cross a hill; it rolls back. At quantum scales, particles do not behave like tiny balls with exact paths. Their state is described by a wave-like probability that can extend into and sometimes beyond an energy barrier. This effect is called quantum tunneling.

The word “tunnel” is a metaphor. A particle does not dig a passage or borrow energy while hidden inside. When its quantum state meets a barrier, the mathematical wave decreases through that region rather than ending sharply at the boundary. If the barrier is thin enough, a nonzero part can remain on the far side. A measurement may then find the particle there. Tunneling probability falls rapidly as a barrier becomes wider or harder to cross. The particle's mass and energy also matter. For everyday objects, the probability is so fantastically small that classical expectations work. At atomic scales, the effect can be important.

Tunneling helps explain radioactive alpha decay, in which a particle escapes a nucleus through a barrier. It also enables scanning tunneling microscopes. When a conducting tip comes extremely close to a surface, electrons can tunnel across the narrow gap. The resulting current changes sensitively with distance, allowing instruments to map surfaces at atomic scale.

The effect does not make every forbidden event possible in practice. It replaces a classical certainty with a probability governed by precise conditions. Quantum tunneling is strange because the far-side result conflicts with the ball-and-hill picture, yet its measured patterns are dependable enough to reveal atoms and support electronic devices.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Quantum tunneling lets particles appear across sufficiently narrow energy barriers with predictable probabilities and important atomic-scale applications.
Quantum particles dig physical holes through barriers by borrowing unlimited energy.
Every everyday object has a high chance of tunneling through a wall.
Barrier width has no effect on the probability of finding a particle beyond it.
questions.explanation: The passage explains the wave-based mechanism, controlling factors, scale, examples, and limits.

questions.stem: Why can a scanning tunneling microscope map tiny surface changes?
choices: Its metal tip digs a groove around every atom.
Its tunneling current responds very strongly to the distance between the tip and surface.
It measures only the motion of ordinary balls over hills.
Its electrons cross any gap with equal probability.
questions.explanation: The application relies on current varying sensitively as the narrow gap changes.

questions.stem: What does “nonzero” mean in the second paragraph?
choices: certain to happen on every measurement
too large to calculate
greater than zero, even if very small
missing from the far side
questions.explanation: Some wave remains beyond the barrier, creating a possible rather than guaranteed measurement there.

questions.stem: Which nuclear process does tunneling help explain?
choices: photosynthesis
magnetic alignment
lunar eclipse
radioactive alpha decay
questions.explanation: The third paragraph directly connects tunneling with radioactive alpha decay.

lesson.strategy: Replace the classical ball path with a wave-like probability, then follow how barrier width changes the far-side chance. Use the two applications to test whether the abstract description is understood.

signals.means: This signals the limit of the familiar classical model at quantum scale.
This identifies how the mathematical state extends within and beyond a barrier.
This guards against interpreting a nonzero probability as practical certainty.

vocab.inContext: a particle being found beyond a barrier its classical energy could not cross
greater than zero even when the amount is extremely small
describing the familiar nonquantum physics that works for everyday objects

skillTips.main-idea: State the main idea through wave probability, barrier conditions, and atomic-scale consequences.
skillTips.inference: Infer microscope sensitivity from how strongly current changes with the tip-to-surface gap.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the possible far-side measurement to define nonzero as small but greater than nothing.
skillTips.detail: For the nuclear example, distinguish alpha decay from the separate microscope application.
